summary: Divisor closure is exact: if m/p = sum of k unit fractions and d | m then (m/d)/p = sum of k unit fractions (divide each denominator by d); checked with 0 violations for all censused numerators m in {1..10,12,16,25} and primes p<30000 (scripts/z52d_p2_TO0b_numer_closure.py; census data/z52b/pass2/TO0b/numer/). Hence ES(p) <=> 4 in M(p) <=> some multiple of 4 in M(p); in the census 4 is representable for all 3244 primes 5<=p<30000, so the first multiple of 4 is 4 itself and nothing new appears.
not_done: Only numerators m <= 25 censused (p < 30000); no test of M(p) beyond 25.

summary: Exact 3-term identities (1 + 1/((p+1)/2) + 1/(p(p+1)/2) = (p+2)/p and 1/1+1/(p+1)+1/(p(p+1)) = (p+1)/p) make m = p+1, p+2 and 2p+1 representable for all 301 primes 5..2000 (scripts/z52d_p2_TO0b_parity_numer.py); for p = 1 mod 4 none of these is 0 mod 4. summary: Identity 4/n = 2/((n+1)/2) + 1/M + 1/M with M = n(n+1)/2 verified exactly for all odd n <= 10001. Note the first term is a numerator-2 fraction with denominator (n+1)/2, not a unit fraction, so this is a weighted identity, not a 3-term unit-fraction identity; the numerator-2 relaxation only changes the problem by one weight.
not_done: Weight vectors (1,1,2), (1,2,3) not explored.

summary: Exact bijection proved: 8/p = sum 1/x_i iff 4/p = sum 1/(2x_i), so 8-solutions correspond one-to-one to all-even 4-solutions. Checked for all 1611 primes p = 1 mod 4 below 30000: the number of 8-solutions equals the number of all-even 4-solutions (es census column 9) for every prime, and existence agrees (scripts/z52d_p2_TO0b_Z0212_bijection.py). The item's 'some denominator = 0 mod 4' variant is not tested as a bijection (it is not an identity).

summary: Premise false as stated: 'odd-denominator ES is impossible' fails. A sum of unit fractions with all denominators odd and equal to 4/n has an even number of terms (2-adic parity, checked: no 3-term odd solutions for odd n <= 301), but two odd terms already work for 969 of the 1500 odd n in [3,3001] (e.g. 4/3 = 1/1 + 1/3 and 4/9 = 1/3 + 1/9, all denominators odd; the 2-term test is the divisor condition on n^2). So the local 2-adic constraint is a parity-of-count constraint, not an impossibility.
